description: What makes things funny, in the substrate's own machinery — so the agent can GROUND humour from trope-play examples rather than have 'funny' hand-coded. Humour is a setup that installs an EXPECTATION (narrative_convention), a BENIGN VIOLATION of it (a subversion the agent already feels as surprise), and a RESOLUTION that reframes the violation so it coheres (a re-compression under a second frame). The agent already has expectation (forward models), surprise (an emotion), and reframing (curiosity/compression); humour is those composed, not a new module. The 'funny' signal is grounded from the surprise-then-resolve shape over examples. Cognitive-science grounding: incongruity-resolution (Suls), script-opposition (Raskin/Attardo GTVH), benign-violation (McGraw & Warren). The setup->violation->resolution mechanism itself belongs as derivation_rules in a humour expansion pack.

concepts.name: incongruity
concepts.definition: Two frames (scripts) that do not fit together — a state the substrate registers as a FAILURE TO COMPRESS under a single frame. The raw material of humour: a setup admits one reading, the punchline forces another that clashes with it.

concepts.name: resolution
concepts.definition: The 'getting it' — finding the SECOND frame under which the incongruity coheres, i.e. a re-compression that makes the clash sensible. Humour requires both the incongruity AND its resolution; an unresolved incongruity is merely confusing, a resolved one without violation is merely clever.

concepts.name: benign_violation
concepts.definition: The violated expectation must be felt as SAFE — a transgression that does not actually threaten. This is what separates a joke from an alarm: the same violated expectation is funny when benign and frightening when not. The benign tag gates the surprise signal into humour rather than fear.

concepts.name: comic_subversion
concepts.definition: The bridge to trope_play: a SUBVERTED (or exaggerated, or lampshaded) convention is the most common engine of humour — the convention installs the expectation, the play-operation supplies the benign violation, and recognising the device supplies the resolution. Most catalogued 'Played for Laughs' examples are this shape.

concepts.name: irony
concepts.definition: A stable gap between the expected/stated meaning and the actual one, held open rather than immediately resolved. Dramatic irony (audience knows what a character does not) is an expectation mismatch ACROSS frames (viewer-frame vs character-frame); verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant, trusting the listener to reframe.

concepts.name: satire_parody_target
concepts.definition: Humour aimed AT something — a work, genre, or convention is set up as the target and its expectations are violated to comment on it. Connects humour to intertextuality (reference Mt): the violated expectation belongs to another work/convention, and the resolution requires recognising the target.
